A note from Cascade Legal Rights Project

Thank you for raising this, and I'm sorry. Whether or not the letters you're describing came from us, receiving a notice from a landlord's lawyer soon after you asked for help is frightening, and everyone here deserves a straight answer about what happens to your information.

What we do with your information

Cascade Legal Rights Project does not share, sell, or otherwise disclose attendee information to landlords or their attorneys, and our policy for staff and volunteers prohibits doing so. Sign-in sheets and intake notes are retained internally, in locked storage, and are accessible only to our staff and volunteer attorneys.

Why those letters may be arriving

Eviction and dispossessory filings in the magistrate courts are public records. Law firms that handle these cases can obtain names and addresses from public filings and use them to mail tenants. That is the most likely explanation for the letters described in this thread: a case filed in court can generate a letter to you without anyone here sharing anything. We can't discuss any individual's situation, including that of our own clients, so we can't confirm the specifics of anyone's letter. If you received one and had not told anyone else about your situation, please contact us and we'll help you look into it.

The clinic is still happening

Saturday, November 14, 10am to 1pm, walk-in, no appointment needed. The library's community meeting room is closed that day for repairs, so the clinic will be at Mt. Zion fellowship hall instead, same hours, 10am to 1pm. Mt. Zion is in East Atlanta, with an accessible side entrance by the parking lot.

You are welcome there. If you'd prefer not to sign anything, you still come and talk with an attorney.

Questions: clinic@cascaderights.example, or call our office at 404-555-0187.

Please come. Asking about your rights is not something you should have to hide.
